plan.p0: One plausible mechanism is diagonal ray completion: identify each diagonal stroke or segment in the input, extend it in both directions to the grid boundaries, and preserve its salient color while suppressing incidental shapes. This fits the observed outputs’ long, uninterrupted diagonals. Distinguishing assumption: every detected segment generates a full ray, even if it is short or isolated.
plan.p1: Another possibility is diagonal-line projection from colored objects: use the positions of non-background objects to infer several parallel diagonals, then redraw those complete diagonals using the object’s associated marker color. This fits the repeated parallel 7, 0, and 7 lines observed. Distinguishing assumption: object geometry determines line offsets, so differently shaped objects could produce different numbers of lines.
plan.p2: A contrasting mechanism is boundary-seeded propagation: begin at diagonal-colored cells touching or approaching a border and propagate them along their slope until the opposite boundary, ignoring interior colors except as direction cues. The outputs are consistent with border-to-border diagonal traces. Distinguishing assumption: only border-connected traces matter; an enclosed diagonal would not be extended.
plan.p3: A fourth possibility is lattice reconstruction: infer a periodic family of diagonal tracks from the spacing of the input marks, then fill every in-bounds cell on those tracks with the relevant output color. This can explain the regular parallel diagonals in both observed outputs. Distinguishing assumption: missing members of the inferred periodic lattice are restored, even when no corresponding input segment exists.
